title: 2010 AMC 12B Problem 14
statement: Let \(a,\) \(b,\) \(c,\) \(d,\) and \(e\) be positive integers with \(a+b+c+d+e=2010,\) and let \(M\) be the largest of the sums \(a+b,\) \(b+c,\) \(c+d,\) and \(d+e.\) What is the smallest possible value of \(M?\)

solutions.text:
Each of \(a+b,\) \(d+e,\) and \(c\) is at most \(M\) (note \(c\le c+d\le M\)). Adding, \(2010=(a+b)+c+(d+e)\) \(\le3M,\) so \(M\ge670.\)

If \(M=670,\) then \(c=670,\) but then \(b+c\ge671\gt M,\) a contradiction. Hence \(M\ge671.\)

The value \(671\) is reached by \((a,b,c,d,e)=\) \((669,1,670,1,669),\) whose consecutive-pair sums are \(670,671,671,670.\)

Thus, the correct answer is B.
hints: \((a+b)+c+(d+e)=2010,\) and each of \(a+b,\) \(c,\) and \(d+e\) is at most \(M\)
This forces \(3M\ge2010;\) rule out \(M=670,\) then build an example reaching the bound
